cards.name: Boston Basin, Sharkfin Col rappel, and south across the Boston Glacier to the schrund
cards.notes:
Start from the Boston Basin trailhead near 3,200 ft, about 21.7 miles up Cascade River Road — a different and shorter drive than the Cascade Pass trailhead used for the southwest route. The climbers' path follows an old overgrown mining road about a mile to a former mine site, then a steep boot path through old growth with roughly four creek crossings, emerging above treeline near 5,300 ft into Boston Basin: about 2.5 miles and 3,100 ft, typically three to four hours. Camp low at about 5,300 ft or high at 6,300-6,400 ft; NPS permit required and camping restricted to the established sites.

From high camp, follow the Quien Sabe Glacier route roped, and climb toward Sharkfin Col rather than taking the loose class 3-4 scramble around Boston Peak. Many parties gain the ridge just east of the col, where a natural or fixed sling anchor is used for a short rappel — or, in leaner conditions, a steep no-fall-zone downclimb on crumbly mixed rock — onto the Boston Glacier. Multiple trip reports flag this as the technical crux of the approach, sometimes harder than the climbing above.

Once on the Boston Glacier, rope up and traverse south toward the base of Buckner's north face, zig-zagging around the schrund and large crevasses near the toe, with some rock scrambling to bypass the gap. Many parties bivy on the glacier itself around 7,800 ft to shorten summit day.

cards.name: Over Sahale and the Boston-Sahale col from Sahale Glacier Camp

cards.name: Aasgard Pass and the Core, fifty feet left of the standard south-face line
cards.notes:
The Core Enchantments approach: Stuart Lake trailhead, Stuart Lake Trail 2.5 miles to the Colchuck Lake Trail junction, across Mountaineer Creek and up the switchbacks to Colchuck Lake at 5,570 ft. From the boulder field at the lake's south end, Aasgard Pass — 1.25 miles gaining about 2,000 ft of steep loose scree and dirt, the physical crux of the approach, with a hidden creek and moat under lingering snow into early July.

From the pass at 7,841 ft, continue cross-country through the upper Core past Isolation and Tranquil Lake toward Prusik Pass and Gnome Tarn. Parties commonly bivy at the tarn, about twenty minutes from the base. There is no maintained trail for the last stretch.

cards.name: Snow Lakes and the lower Enchantments
cards.notes: The longer, more gradual way in from Icicle Creek Road: the Snow Lakes trail climbs past Nada and Snow lakes to Lake Vivianne, about ten miles with well over 5,000 ft of gain, looking straight at Prusik's south face. From Vivianne continue past the upper lakes to the base of the south face. It avoids the loose grind of Aasgard Pass at the cost of roughly two more miles and a thousand more feet. It is also the fallback when Aasgard or the trailhead is closed. From Lake Viviane, go up and right toward Temple Lake and then up climbers' paths through boulders to the base of the south face.

cards.name: Aasgard Pass to Gnome Tarn
cards.notes:
Stuart Lake Trailhead, Colchuck Lake Trail #1599A across Mountaineer Creek and up the switchbacks to Colchuck Lake at 5,570 ft — about four miles and 2,000-2,200 ft.

From the boulder field at the lake's south end, climb Aasgard Pass: roughly 2,000 ft in a little over a mile of loose scree and dirt, and the crux of the day. Stay climber's left of the cliff bands; the terrain to climber's right, toward the waterfalls on Colchuck Peak's flank, cliffs out and has killed people. Snow lingering into early July hides a creek running beneath the talus.

From the pass at 7,841 ft travel cross-country through the Core, dropping from Talisman Lake toward Rune Lake, then ascending to the gentle ridge east of Rune's upper basin to reach Gnome Tarn. Gnome Tarn is the standard camp for this face and sits close under it.

The last stretch to the wall is unmarked cross-country over slabs and talus.

cards.name: Trail #1587 from US-2 to the Nason Ridge crest
cards.notes: One of the steepest maintained trails near Stevens Pass, and it starts working immediately. From the dirt pullout on the north side of the highway the tread climbs on an old service road beneath powerlines, leaves the roadbed at a signed bend about a third of a mile up, and then runs into ninety-odd tight switchbacks on an open south-facing slope with no shade at all. Schilling Creek near the bottom is the only accessible water on the climb and it drops away quickly, so fill everything at the car and carry three litres or more. The grade eases into heather meadows around 2.8 miles and the tread tops out on the crest at about 6,000 ft.

cards.name: Snowy Creek trail from Smith Brook road
cards.notes: Drive Smith Brook road six miles and the narrow, brushy Snowy Creek road a further three and a half to a small trailhead with very limited parking. The trail follows Snowy Creek through old growth, then climbs to the crest and joins the main route about half a mile short of the summit. It is shorter and far less steep than the highway trail. The Snowy Creek road has been closed by storm damage since June 2026, so check before driving it.

cards.name: Park Creek Pass and the heather traverse to the Fremont saddle and the hogsback
cards.notes:
The standard start is the Colonial Creek Campground trailhead on SR-20 near milepost 130, about 1,060-1,200 ft, and the Thunder Creek trail south for roughly 16-18 miles to the Thunder Basin camp area around 6,000 ft and on to Park Creek Pass.

From Park Creek Pass leave the maintained trail and traverse gradually northward around a broad ridge through open heather and high alpine terrain, roughly a mile and a half to two miles, crossing a rib around 7,600 ft and a steep gully through cliff bands around 7,350 ft that can hold snow or ice. That brings you to the Fremont Glacier saddle around 8,000-8,250 ft, where rock-outcrop bivy sites with nearby running water make the standard high camp.

From camp it is about three and a half hours to the summit.

cards.name: Stehekin and the Park Creek trail to Park Creek Pass
cards.notes: From the Park Creek Trailhead on the Stehekin Valley Road, the Park Creek trail climbs to Park Creek Pass and joins the Thunder Creek line there. It needs the Lake Chelan boat and the Stehekin shuttle to reach the trailhead. The way in starts at the High Bridge guard station near 1,600 ft, follows the Stehekin River trail to the Park Creek trailhead, then takes the Park Creek trail past Buckner Camp, with a creek crossing on a less-than-substantial footlog that is genuinely nerve-wracking in the dark.

cards.name: White River Trail #1507 and the old sheep path into Thunder Basin
cards.notes: From Coles Corner take Hwy 207 toward Lake Wenatchee, then White River Road (FR-6400) to its end at the White River / Indian Creek Trailhead near 2,300 ft. Hike White River Trail #1507 about six miles to the Thunder Creek crossing; there is an established camp right at the crossing. Half a mile past Thunder Creek the maintained trail is left behind for an old, unmaintained sheep path that climbs the west side of the Thunder Creek drainage. This is the hard part of the walk in: avalanche debris, blowdown, and dense slide alder choking the tread below the lower basin. Above the alder it opens into a lower basin near 4,175 ft and then climbs steeply into Thunder Basin, an open basin of granite slabs and small tarns which is the standard high camp and has a direct view of the peak. The flat upper basin is near 5,200 ft; the granite slabs and two small tarns at the top of the basin, near 6,400-6,500 ft, are a higher camp closer to the col.

cards.name: North Fork Sauk Trail, the PCT and Boulder Pass from the west
cards.notes: A far longer way in comes from the west: North Fork Sauk Trail #649 past Mackinaw Shelter to the PCT, then cross-country over Boulder Pass and through the Napeequa to the peak's north and north-east side. Parties who have done it report twenty-plus stream crossings and heavy brush over three days. It is a different trip, not a shortcut.

cards.name: Middle Fork Nooksack Road (FR-38) and Rankin Creek to the treeline camp, then the southwest basin
cards.notes:
This is the more direct way to the X Couloir: from the south via the Middle Fork Nooksack River Road (FR-38). The southwest face can also be reached by a less direct line with more glacier travel; do not confuse either with the north-facing Coleman side, which leads to the other route on this mountain.

Drive FR-38 toward its mile-12.5 switchback and start walking the old decommissioned road around Point 4481 toward Rankin Creek. Snow travel — often by bike or snowshoe on the lower stretch — leads past East Rankin Lake near 5,120 ft and up into the basin to a sheltered camp at treeline around 6,100 ft, by the highest trees in the basin below Seward Peak. Roughly seven miles and 3,350 ft of gain to camp.

Access: FR-38, damaged in the December 2025 floods, has been closed to vehicles at milepost 7 by a washout since July 27, 2026, with no end date given on the Mt. Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest alert still posted on September 26, 2026, and a separate gate at Wallace Creek near mile 10 closes the road 1 December to 15 June for elk calving. Confirm the drivable road-end with the Mount Baker Ranger District before the trip; the length of the approach varies year to year.

cards.name: Heliotrope Ridge and the Thunder Glacier cirque
cards.notes: Start at the Heliotrope Ridge trailhead and follow the trail toward the old cabin site, then rope up and cross the lower glaciers south into the Thunder Glacier cirque to reach the southwest side of the peak. It is less direct than the Rankin Creek line, with much more glacier travel, but it starts from a paved-to-gravel road that is usually open when the Middle Fork road is not.

cards.name: Cosho Camp to the 7,830 ft saddle and the north snowfield
cards.notes: From Cosho Camp continue west down the Fisher Creek Trail about a mile and leave it at one of the gullies due south of the Cosho-Kimtah saddle, starting around 3,800 ft. The climb up is the crux of the day: sustained bushwhacking through trees and brush for the first thousand feet, then loose, tedious scree and steep grass with occasional solid rock, roughly 4,000 ft of gain to the saddle at about 7,830 ft.

cards.name: From Kimtah, down the south gully and the connecting traverse
cards.notes: This way is used by parties combining Cosho with Kimtah: they descend Kimtah's south gully and follow cairns down the connecting traverse to the same saddle.

cards.name: North Fork Entiat Trail #1437 to the meadow camp
cards.notes: Drive the Entiat River Road and then the switchbacking forest-road spur to the North Fork Entiat Trailhead, and follow North Fork Entiat River Trail #1437 up-valley. Almost all of the distance to the peak is on trail. The usual staging point is the trail camp in the meadow below the summit around 6,700 ft, and the climb starts from the tread a short way north of it. The base-finding below is written for this trail camp side.

cards.name: Emerald Park trail from Lucerne
cards.notes: Take the boat up Lake Chelan to Lucerne, follow the Domke Lake trail to the Emerald Park trail, and climb up Emerald Park to Milham Pass, which drops into the basin between Emerald and Saska. A boat-dependent alternative to the Entiat side, and the natural choice when coming from Lake Chelan. It reaches the peak from Emerald Park via Trail #1230 out of the lakeshore settlement. Where this line joins the climbing is unclear.

why: Card 1 narrates the Holden/Copper Basin and Cottonwood/Entiat Glacier ways in, which have their own cards.

cards.name: Phelps Creek and Leroy Basin, over the col and across the Gloomy Glacier
cards.notes:
Same walk in as for Seven Fingered Jack and Maude: Phelps Creek trail to the Leroy Creek crossing at about 4,140 ft, then the steep unmaintained climbers' trail on the north side of the creek into Leroy Basin at about 6,100 ft.

This is the common approach but not the elegant one. All three ways in converge on the same south-east face finish.

From Leroy Basin, head north-west toward a waterfall and climb its left side to a small notch on the ridge of Seven Fingered Jack. Published descriptions of this saddle vary — one places it just west of an obvious 7,700 ft col with a couple of bivy sites at the low point, another gives it as a notch reached past a second creek crossing — and they may or may not be the same feature, so check it on a map rather than assuming.

From the saddle you must drop about a thousand feet into the moraine at the terminus of the Gloomy Glacier, and every foot of it has to be regained on the way out. Two published ways down: descend to the tarn below and go around a prominent rock formation that guards the basin, or descend to the right across sandy ledges and down large boulders.

Expect roughly nine hours round trip from Leroy Basin, and a very long day car to car — one party left the trailhead at three in the morning and got back at eleven at night.

cards.name: Holden Village and Copper Basin
cards.notes: From Holden Village up to the Copper–Entiat divide and the east ridge. The most direct way to the standard east-side line, and climbable in a day from Holden, but it depends on the Lake Chelan boat. The ferry up Lake Chelan to Holden and the Railroad Creek trail into Copper Basin gains the East Ridge — the standard route — much more directly than the Leroy Basin approach.

cards.name: Entiat River from Cottonwood
cards.notes: Up the Entiat River trail toward the Entiat Glacier and the east ridge. The longest way in, with less gain and little avalanche exposure. It reaches the East Ridge by way of the Entiat Glacier.

why: Card 1 narrates the War Creek Ridge / Williams Creek way in, which has its own card.

cards.name: Reynolds Creek Trail and the South Fork drainage
cards.notes: The short way in, and short is relative. From the road end off the Twisp River an unmaintained primitive trail climbs through forest alongside the creek for roughly three miles. Above the confluence the tread gives out and about two miles of intermittent bushwhacking through slide alder, downed timber and a boot path that comes and goes is the real crux of the day — several parties lose more time here than on the mountain. The basin above holds snow well into summer, so an axe is worth carrying even when the valley looks dry. Mark the point where you leave the tread; it is easy to miss coming down.

cards.name: Williams Lake and War Creek Ridge
cards.notes: Longer, but on good trail at first and far more scenic. From the Williams Creek trailhead on the West Twisp River road at about 2,800 ft, follow the well-marked trail to Williams Lake at about 6,500 ft, then climb over Williams Butte and follow War Creek Ridge toward Camel's Hump. Drop through a boulder break in the cliffs into the upper South Fork Reynolds Creek basin and climb heather and scree to the summit pyramid. It can be strung into a loop with a neighbouring summit, and it joins the same finish as the Reynolds Creek way.

The basin above holds snow well into summer, so an axe is worth carrying even when the valley looks dry. A longer alternative comes in over War Creek Ridge from the Williams Creek side and can be strung into a loop with a neighbouring summit, but it joins the same finish. Mark the point where you leave the tread; it is easy to miss coming down.

orig.name: Williams Lake and War Creek Ridge
orig.notes: Longer, but on good trail at first and far more scenic. From the Williams Creek trailhead on the West Twisp River road at about 2,800 ft, follow the well-marked trail to Williams Lake at about 6,500 ft, then climb over Williams Butte and follow War Creek Ridge toward Camel's Hump. Drop through a boulder break in the cliffs into the upper South Fork Reynolds Creek basin and climb heather and scree to the summit pyramid.

why: Card 1 narrates the Cougar Creek / North Fork Sauk way in from FR 49 (fords, hazards); no card for it.

cards.name: Bedal Creek to the Southwest Face basin
cards.notes:
Bedal Creek is the preferred trailhead for this side of the peak because it avoids the river fords. FR 4096 off the Mountain Loop Highway, about 18.25 miles south of Darrington and roughly a mile south of Bedal Campground; the spur is rough and narrow. Trailhead about 2,790 ft.

Bedal Creek Trail #705 through old growth and along the creek's steep banks until the tread ends at a large washout, roughly one and a half to two and a half miles in. Scramble the washout to a cairned exit onto the climbers' path, which leaves left near 48.0560, -121.3631 around 3,500 ft under pink flagging and switchbacks steeply up to about 4,900 ft. Talus and meadow then lead to the 5,300 ft Bedal-Sloan saddle — last reliable water before the wall.

This is a full day of walking before a long rock route.

cards.name: Cougar Creek and the North Fork Sauk from FR 49
cards.notes: This way starts from FR 49 and reaches the same basin from the north. It requires fording the North Fork Sauk plus a cold Cougar Creek crossing, slide alder and devil's club.

why: Card 1 narrates the Merritt Lake trail way in from the west; no card for it.

cards.name: Round Mountain Trail #1529 to Nason Ridge and the lookout spur
cards.notes: From the highway just past the rest area, turn north onto the unsigned Butcher Creek Road (Forest Road 6910) — the turn is on a curve with fast traffic, so watch for it — and follow good gravel a few miles before turning onto the short spur that ends at the Round Mountain Trailhead. Round Mountain Trail #1529 climbs steeply for about a mile and a half through forest and an older burn to its junction with Nason Ridge Trail #1583. Turn left and west and follow the ridge trail, which undulates along the crest for a few miles to the lookout spur.

cards.name: Merritt Lake trail from the west
cards.notes: A longer way in reaches the same ridge trail from the west via the Merritt Lake trail. It is used mainly for through-hikes or when the Round Mountain side is inaccessible.

why: Card 1 narrates the Entiat River / Myrtle Lake / Cow Creek Pass way in, which has its own card.

cards.name: Basalt Ridge crest to Fifth of July Pass
cards.notes: This is the shorter alternative to the Entiat River approach. From the Basalt Pass trailhead, climb to the pass — the small stream in the gully below it is the last water, and there is none at all beyond — then follow the ridge north. The trail bypasses the first high point about 300 ft below it, and beyond the trail fork the tread fades into slick pumice. Continue north past the neighbouring tower's saddle, then through a col around 7,480 ft on the next peak's southwest ridge, dropping through a scree gully into the basin west of it. Hop the massive boulders in that basin, cross a small larch meadow, and regain the ridge. The marks below are written for this Basalt Ridge side.

cards.name: Entiat River and Larch Lakes
cards.notes: From the trailhead at the end of the Entiat River road, follow the Entiat River trail up the valley and climb the side trail to the Larch Lakes meadows. From a camp between the lakes the summit is a modest day out along the ridge. Longer than the Basalt Ridge line, but on maintained trail with water, so it suits multi-day trips and loops. The Entiat River side goes by way of Myrtle Lake, the Larch Lakes and Cow Creek Pass; that is the line the main approach and waypoints describe.

why: Card 1 narrates the Crater Creek / Eagle Lake alternative, which has its own card.

cards.name: Foggy Dew Creek and Merchants Basin to Cooney Lake
cards.notes: Most parties backpack in and camp at one of the lakes rather than push the whole eighteen to twenty mile round trip in a day. From the Foggy Dew road end the trail climbs the North Fork past a two-tiered cascade — the last easy water before the country opens — and tops out of the timber into a wildflower basin below the ridge, where a spur trail branches toward the lake. Above the lake the ground is dry, so fill there. Larches turn gold around the basin in late September, which is a fine but colder window with a real chance of early snow icing the summit blocks.

cards.name: Crater Creek and the Eagle Lakes side
cards.notes: A higher start at about 4,760 ft and a gentler grade, with a creek ford. From the Crater Creek trailhead follow the Eagle Lakes trail a little over two miles, then the Martin Creek trail to the Cooney Lake trail; parties can also base at Upper Eagle Lake and cross Horsehead Pass. Often used to make a loop with the Foggy Dew side. A signed cutoff leads south past a second set of lakes to reach the same lake basin as the Foggy Dew side.

why: Card 1 narrates the Spider Gap / Railroad Creek / Holden Village way in; no card for it.

cards.name: Phelps Creek Trail #1511 to Spider Meadow and upper Phelps Basin
cards.notes:
From the Phelps Creek Trailhead at about 3,500 ft at the end of FR-6211, follow Phelps Creek Trail #1511 north up the east side of the creek. It climbs gently — roughly 1,900 ft over five or six miles — through old and second growth, with several small side streams giving reliable water the whole way. After a heavy avalanche winter the tread threads graveyards of downed timber pushed across it from the slopes to the west.

Spider Meadow near 5,150-5,400 ft is the last easy, reliable water. Walk the length of the meadow to its head, where the trail forks. The fork is unsigned: the left branch carries on toward Spider Gap and Larch Knob, and the Dumbell path is the right-hand one, an old climbers' trail into lower Phelps Basin. Most parties camp in the basin around 5,700 to 6,000 ft.

Note that FR-6200 has been closed beyond Atkinson Flat under a storm-damage order, which blocks the drive to this trailhead entirely.

cards.name: Spider Gap from Railroad Creek and Lyman Lake (Holden Village)
cards.notes: A longer alternate reaches the same basin from the east over Spider Gap from Railroad Creek and Lyman Lake out of Holden Village. It is used by parties already doing that loop, not as a way in.

why: Card 1 gives the Thirtymile trailhead location and shuttle, which belongs on the Thirtymile card.

cards.name: Andrews Creek trail #504 from the Chewuch River road
cards.notes:
Drive north from Winthrop up the Chewuch River road to the Andrews Creek trailhead at about 3,080 ft, roughly a five-hour drive from Seattle and the shortest drive of the three ways in.

Walk Andrews Creek trail #504 up the drainage. The lower miles pass through an old burn, so there is little shade and the tread can be overgrown and wet after rain, but the creek is beside you and reliable. The trail tops out at Andrews Pass above 6,680 ft, where the burn gives way to open parkland.

Continue on the Boundary Trail #533 and drop on the Cathedral Lakes side trail to Upper Cathedral Lake at about 7,380 ft. Published figures for the whole walk from this trailhead are about nineteen miles with 5,550 ft of gain, and everyone splits it over at least two days.

Of the three trailheads this one has the shortest drive and the most walking gain.

One thing to leave alone: there is a shorter-looking approach from the Canadian side. Crossing into the United States here is illegal, the border is patrolled, and the fines are severe.

cards.name: Cathedral Driveway trail #510A from Loomis via Toats Coulee
cards.notes:
This is a trail, #510A, and not a four-wheel-drive road, despite a persistent claim to the contrary — the high-clearance warning in circulation belongs to the Iron Gate spur, a different road. Access is from Loomis by Toats Coulee Road, then a Y junction, then NF-39 and NF-300 to the trailhead at about 5,570 ft.

Be careful with the trailhead name. It appears in print as Cathedral Driveway, Chewuch, and Chewack Driveway, and the Chewuch name also belongs to a completely different trailhead near Winthrop. Navigate to the road, not the name.

The Cathedral Driveway descends from its trailhead to join the Chewuch trail #510 around mile 4.8 at about 4,300 ft, and from there it is the Chewuch valley to the Cathedral Lakes basin. Total is about seventeen and a half miles with roughly 3,700 ft of gain — the shortest walk and the least climbing of the three approaches.

The catch is at both ends. The drive is about two hours longer than from Winthrop, and because the trailhead sits high and the trail drops to meet the Chewuch, you finish the trip with roughly 1,300 ft of climbing on the way out, at the point when you least want it.

cards.name: Thirtymile Trailhead and the Chewuch River trail toward Remmel Lake
cards.notes: Follow the Chewuch River trail north from the Thirtymile Trailhead nearly to Remmel Lake, then climb to the Cathedral Lakes basin. A longer way round than Andrews Creek, used when combining the Remmel Lake country with the climb. The Thirtymile trailhead is only about five and a half miles further along the same road than the Andrews Creek trailhead, which makes a car shuttle between them easy.

why: Card 1 narrates picking up the loop from the Grove of the Patriarchs end via the Eastside Trail, which has its own card.

cards.name: Silver Falls loop from the Ohanapecosh side
cards.notes:
This is a single roadside boulder at about 1,900 ft in old forest, not an alpine objective, and the approach is a walk on maintained trail with essentially no gain.

From the Ohanapecosh day-use area, follow the Silver Falls Loop about a mile. Check which end of the loop is open rather than assuming either.

The road serving this corner of the park is seasonal: normally open from late spring through fall and gated in winter.

No climbing permit is involved. The park's climbing permit and its blue-bag rules apply to parties travelling on glaciers or above 10,000 ft, which this is not; the park entrance fee still applies.

cards.name: Eastside Trail from the Grove of the Patriarchs lot
cards.notes: Park at the Grove of the Patriarchs lot on the Stevens Canyon Road, cross the road to the Eastside Trail and follow it about half a mile to the Silver Falls Trail, then continue south toward the falls; the boulder is a few feet off the trail. This is the way in whenever the campground end of the loop is closed, and during that closure the loop cannot be walked through, so come back the way you went. The Grove itself stays closed behind its damaged bridge, but the lot and the Eastside Trail are open in season. The loop can also be picked up from this end, and that corridor has been under reconstruction in recent seasons.

why: Card 1 last paragraph narrates the Thirtymile and Cathedral Driveway ways in, which have their own cards.

cards.name: Andrews Creek trail #504 to Upper Cathedral Lake, then the trail toward Cathedral Pass
cards.notes:
Drive north from Winthrop up the Chewuch River road to the Andrews Creek trailhead at about 3,050 ft and walk trail #504 up the drainage to Andrews Pass above 6,680 ft. The lower half is an old burn with no shade and brushy tread. From the pass, drop into the next drainage and take the Cathedral Lakes trail up to Upper Cathedral Lake at about 7,380 ft. That is the base camp and it is a full long day of walking, usually two.

One early-season bonus is worth planning around: the chasm that splits the summit rocks is often snow-filled early, which makes the first step-across easy or trivial. Late season means a bare hole and the pure version of the move. It can snow here in any month, so carry layers whatever the forecast says.

cards.name: Cathedral Driveway trail #510A from Loomis via Toats Coulee
cards.notes: From the Cathedral Driveway Trailhead on the Toats Coulee road out of Loomis, the trail drops to join the Chewuch trail and then climbs the valley to the Cathedral Lakes basin. The eastern way in, with less climbing than Andrews Creek. It is the trail from the high trailhead above Loomis, not the longer Iron Gate route. It walks the least but drives the longest, and leaves you 1,300 ft of climbing on the way out.

cards.notes: Follow the Chewuch River trail north from the Thirtymile Trailhead nearly to Remmel Lake, then climb to the Cathedral Lakes basin. A longer way round than Andrews Creek, used when combining the Remmel Lake country with the climb. The valley trail is gentle.

why: Card 1 narrates walking the East Bank Trail from SR 20, which has its own card.

cards.name: Ross Lake to May Creek and the Nohokomeen Glacier
cards.notes: A genuinely remote three-day outing on a mountain that sees almost no traffic, and the approach is the hard part of it. Parties reach May Creek Camp on the east shore of Ross Lake at about 1,600 ft far more often by taking the resort water taxi, which removes nearly all of the East Bank Trail walk from SR 20. From the lake it is a few thousand feet of steep forest, and the trick is finding the open timber rather than fighting brush: parties who get it right leave the trail in open forest a couple of hundred yards from the junction, angle left of the fall line, and follow game trails through the rock bands between roughly 3,500 and 4,100 ft, where a short cliff step sometimes carries webbing left behind by earlier parties. Reaching the ridge crest around 5,000 ft, traverse to the top of the moraine, pass under the toe of the Nohokomeen Glacier and climb slabs on its left side to camp at about 6,700 ft. Some parties push on and camp higher on the glacier near 7,400 ft. The glacier above is usually straightforward and largely crack-free to its top at about 8,000 ft. Most parties climb this ridge and descend the East Ridge, which turns the trip into a traverse and puts the exit out to Jerry Lakes and the Crater Mountain trail rather than back down the timber.

cards.name: East Bank Trail on foot to May Creek
cards.notes: Walk the East Bank Trail from SR-20 north along the east shore of Ross Lake to May Creek Camp, where climbers leave the trail. Several hours of flat walking each way, but it needs no booking and works whenever the highway is open. The walk is seven or eight flat miles.

why: Card 1 narrates the Slate Pass / Ferguson Lake trail way in, which has its own card.

cards.name: Lake of the Woods camp and the east ridge
cards.notes: There is no trail on the mountain itself; the whole climb is talus, scree and boulder-field walking off a high camp. The usual staging is a camp around 6,600 ft near Lake of the Woods, reached over Pistol Pass on the long-abandoned Pistol Ridge tread out of the Monument Creek valley. That approach has been unmaintained for decades and involves an unbridged ford of Eureka Creek that runs thigh to waist deep during snowmelt. From camp the peak is a couple of hours each way for a fit party, and most parties pair it with Monument Peak.

cards.name: Slate Pass and the Pasayten side
cards.notes: Start high at Slate Pass on the Harts Pass road and drop toward the Middle Fork Pasayten, then work east by Eureka Creek and around into the basin below the peak. Longer and more cross-country than Pistol Pass, but it starts thousands of feet higher. It reaches the same country by way of the Ferguson Lake trail and avoids the Eureka Creek ford, at the cost of tread that is harder still to follow.

why: Card 1 narrates the West Fork Methow / PCT / Horse Heaven Camp way in, which has its own card.

cards.name: Mill Creek and the Azurite Pass side
cards.notes: This is the approach the peak is normally catalogued under and the one that pairs naturally with Azurite. It runs from Highway 20 up Canyon Creek and then Mill Creek on tread that has seen little maintenance since the mine closed, where slide alder and downed timber are the recurring complaint and parties routinely lose the path entirely for stretches. Camp is usually made near the old mine or in the basin above it. Note that the point long marked on maps as Mount Ballard is a lower north sub-summit; the true high point lies about 1,100 ft further south and is slightly higher.

cards.name: South Fork Slate Creek and the east ridge
cards.notes: The other side of the mountain, approached from the Slate Creek road system rather than from Mill Creek, and the line most parties who climb this peak actually use. It is shorter, the forest below camp is comparatively brush-free, and the route-finding above camp is far more legible than on the Mill Creek side, at the cost of one genuinely steep step low down and some exposed ledge work near the top. Snow conditions change this route's character completely: a filled-in slot low down and firm snow in the upper cirque make for fast travel, while dry late-season conditions leave loose rock and slippery vegetation. Camp is normally made in a scree basin below the east ridge.

cards.name: West Fork Methow and the PCT
cards.notes: From the West Fork Methow trailhead, up to the Pacific Crest Trail by way of Horse Heaven Camp and over to the Mill Creek side. Longer, and usually chosen for combined trips despite the extra mileage.

orig.name: Mill Creek and the Azurite Pass side
orig.notes: This is the approach the peak is normally catalogued under and the one that pairs naturally with Azurite. A longer alternative from the West Fork Methow trailhead reaches the same country by way of the Pacific Crest Trail and Horse Heaven Camp and is often preferred for combined trips despite the extra mileage. Camp is usually made near the old mine or in the basin above it. Note that the point long marked on maps as Mount Ballard is a lower north sub-summit; the true high point lies about 1,100 ft further south and is slightly higher.

orig.name: South Fork Slate Creek and the east ridge
orig.notes: The other side of the mountain, approached from the Slate Creek road system rather than from Mill Creek, and the line most parties who climb this peak actually use. It is shorter, the forest below camp is comparatively brush-free, and the route-finding above camp is far more legible than on the Mill Creek side, at the cost of one genuinely steep step low down and some exposed ledge work near the top. Snow conditions change this route's character completely: a filled-in slot low down and firm snow in the upper cirque make for fast travel, while dry late-season conditions leave loose rock and slippery vegetation. Camp is normally made in a scree basin below the east ridge.

orig.name: West Fork Methow and the PCT
orig.notes: Up the West Fork Methow to the Pacific Crest Trail and over to the Mill Creek side. Longer, and usually chosen for combined trips.

why: Card 1 narrates the Slate Pass / Buckskin Ridge / Ferguson Lake trail ways in, which have their own card.

cards.name: Lower Monument Basin and the left-angling ramp
cards.notes: Monument is the most rugged thing in this group and sits nearly as an island, with Eureka Creek wrapping three sides of it. The travelled approach is the Monument Creek trail from the Lost River road: well maintained through old growth for about four miles to the Eureka Creek confluence, then unmaintained, brushy and deadfall-choked, with a ford of Eureka Creek that can run thigh to waist deep in early summer. From there the abandoned tread climbs onto Pistol Ridge and over Pistol Pass, and most parties camp near Lake of the Woods. Summit day is long enough that finishing the last talus by headlamp is common.

cards.name: From Slate Pass by Robinson Creek and the Ferguson Lake trail
cards.notes: Gentler, though not shorter. Drop north from Slate Pass to the Robinson Creek trail along the Middle Fork Pasayten, then near the big meadow horse camp take the Ferguson Lake trail, which descends about seven miles to Eureka Creek just south of the peak. From there, pick a line up the south side or into the basin between Monument and Lake Mountain. Three approaches off Slate Pass and Buckskin Ridge use the Ferguson Lake trail and reach the same basin from the north.
